title: Poles and zeros of a transfer function

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Replace \(j\omega\) by the complex frequency \(s\) and a transfer function becomes a ratio of polynomials \(H(s) = N(s)/D(s)\). The roots of the numerator are **zeros** (where \(H = 0\)) and the roots of the denominator are **poles** (where \(H\) blows up). Plotted on the \(s\)-plane, they summarize the whole system.

Poles set the natural behaviour: a pole at \(s = -\alpha\) gives a decaying term \(e^{-\alpha t}\) in the response. Poles in the left half-plane mean the system is stable; a pole in the right half-plane means the response grows without bound. Complex-conjugate pole pairs give oscillation inside a decaying envelope. The frequency response is just \(H(s)\) evaluated along the imaginary axis.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ H(s) = K\,\frac{(s - z_1)(s - z_2)\cdots}{(s - p_1)(s - p_2)\cdots} \]
A real pole at \(s = -\omega_p\) gives a corner at \(\omega = \omega_p\) in the frequency response and the time constant \(\tau = 1/\omega_p\).
Stability: every pole must satisfy \(\operatorname{Re}(p_k) < 0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Find the poles and zeros of
\[ H(s) = \frac{10\,(s + 50)}{s^2 + 1100\,s + 10^{5}} \]
Zero: \(s = -50\). Poles: factor \(s^2 + 1100s + 10^5 = (s + 100)(s + 1000)\), so \(s = -100\) and \(s = -1000\). All are in the left half-plane, so the system is stable. The step response contains \(e^{-100t}\) and \(e^{-1000t}\) terms; the slower one (time constant 10 ms) dominates the settling.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Sign slips: a factor \((s + 100)\) means a pole at \(s = -100\), not \(+100\).
- Calling a zero in the right half-plane unstable. Only poles decide stability.
- Forgetting a pole or zero at the origin hidden in an \(s\) factor.
- Confusing the pole location (rad/s) with a frequency in Hz.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Poles and zeros connect the time domain (decaying exponentials and ringing) with the frequency domain (corners on a Bode plot). They are central to feedback stability, where a loop's extra poles decide whether an amplifier rings or oscillates.
